title: PropInsight
excerpt: A configurable web scraper that extracts real-estate listing prices and attributes from property portals into clean, structured data (CSV, JSON, or database).
full_description:
PropInsight is a configurable web scraper whose single job is to collect real-estate listing prices and turn them into clean, structured data. It walks the result pages of a property portal, opens each listing, extracts a consistent set of fields — asking price, price per square metre, location, property type, area, number of rooms, condition, listing date and the listing URL — and writes them out as CSV, JSON, or straight into a database table. What it deliberately does not do is decide what the numbers mean: it is the data-collection layer, not a valuation product.

Each supported portal is described by a declarative site profile — a small config file that maps the portal's page structure to PropInsight's common schema, listing the search-results selector, the pagination rule, and a selector (or regex) per output field. Adding a new portal, or repairing one after a redesign, means editing that profile rather than writing new code, which matters because listing sites change their markup often and without warning. Simple, server-rendered sites are fetched over plain HTTP; sites that build their listings in JavaScript fall back to a headless browser automatically.

Scrapes are meant to be repeated, not run once. PropInsight stores every run as a timestamped snapshot rather than overwriting the previous result, so the history falls out of the data for free: a listing whose price appears three times at three different values has been reduced twice, and a listing that stops appearing has either sold or been withdrawn. Runs are idempotent and resumable — an interrupted scrape picks up where it stopped instead of starting the crawl again — and each row keeps the URL and fetch timestamp it came from so any figure can be traced back to its source page.

The output is intentionally boring and portable. A CSV drops into a spreadsheet, the JSON feeds a script or a notebook, and the SQLite/Postgres writer gives a queryable price history without any extra infrastructure. Typical uses: tracking asking prices in a specific neighbourhood over months before buying; building a personal dataset of comparable sales to sanity-check an agent's valuation; watching a fixed set of listings for price drops; or feeding a spreadsheet model or BI tool that expects tabular input.

Network egress is pluggable. Out of the box requests leave from the machine running the scrape, but PropInsight can also route them through a proxy pool — a handful of static proxies, a datacenter provider, or a commercial residential proxy service (Bright Data, Oxylabs, Smartproxy and similar all expose the same rotating HTTP/SOCKS endpoint, so they drop in as a config value rather than a code change). Residential exit nodes matter for two practical reasons: large portals routinely block whole datacenter IP ranges outright regardless of how slowly you crawl, and many listing sites serve different prices, currencies or inventory depending on the visitor's country, so scraping a foreign market accurately means exiting from it. The proxy layer supports per-request or per-session rotation, sticky sessions where a portal ties results to a session cookie, geo-targeting by country or city, and automatic retry through a different exit node when one gets blocked or times out.

It is built to scrape politely and stay on the right side of the sites it reads: it honours robots.txt, rate-limits itself with configurable delays and concurrency caps, identifies itself with a real user agent, and caches pages so that re-running a scrape during development does not mean re-hitting the server. The intended scope is personal research and small-scale market analysis — not bulk republication of someone else's listing database. Proxies are a routing tool, not a licence to hammer a site: rate limits, delays and concurrency caps apply per-target regardless of how many exit nodes are in the pool, so adding proxies never increases the load an individual portal sees.

title: StockSentinel
excerpt: Personal stock watchlist and portfolio tracker with real-time price alerts, on-demand news feed, and automated email decision prompts.
full_description: StockSentinel is a web-based stock tracker and alert system for self-directed investors. You build a list of tickers — marking each as Watching (candidate) or Holding (position you own, with cost basis and quantity) — and the app monitors them continuously in real time. When a configured alert condition fires (e.g. a 20% intraday drop), you receive an email within seconds, not at the end of the day. Charts cover the full historical range of a stock with timeframe selectors from 1D to All, and a dedicated Historical Analysis view lets you explore the lowest and highest points a stock ever reached, with annotations marking when they occurred. An on-demand News panel fetches the latest headlines from the past 3 months (via Google News RSS) for any ticker, shown only when the user explicitly requests it. All values display in EUR or USD.

title: SmartBOM Optimizer
excerpt: AI tool that reads a BOM exported from any major PCB design tool, detects duplicate or near-equivalent components, and proposes part-number consolidations with a projected € savings estimate.
full_description:
Hardware teams routinely end up with BOMs full of near-duplicate components — the same resistor value sourced under three different part numbers, or capacitors with equivalent specs scattered across a project because different engineers each picked their own. Reviewing this manually is slow but valuable: on large projects with multiple BOMs and thousands of components, consolidating parts can produce real, immediately visible savings.

SmartBOM Optimizer automates that review, working entirely from the BOM itself with no external supplier or pricing database required. It ingests a BOM exported from any of the leading PCB design tools, has AI scan every line for repeated or near-identical components (same value within tolerance, equivalent footprint/specs, same or overlapping manufacturer), and groups them into consolidation candidates. Each group is scored by confidence — exact duplicates can be merged with one click, near-equivalents are flagged for review, and inconsistencies (like a stray 0.1% tolerance part among a batch of 1% parts) are surfaced as informational flags rather than forced merges.

Review happens at the individual component-line level, not just the group level: a user can expand any group and choose exactly which lines to merge, since some duplicates are intentional (e.g. a deliberate second source). Lines left unmerged can be marked as an intentional exception so the tool remembers the decision and stops re-flagging it on future runs of the same BOM. A KPI summary — duplicate groups found, lines consolidated before/after, distinct PNs before/after — gives an immediate sense of impact, with an € savings figure shown (grayed out if unavailable) only when the input BOM already includes a cost column, since fabricating a savings number without real pricing data would undermine trust in the tool.

Connected to a company's ERP/PLM system (e.g. SAP) — live via API or through a periodically exported list of approved/in-stock components — the same engine can also restrict suggestions to parts that are already approved and in stock, turning it from a spreadsheet trick into a genuine sourcing tool. The value is easy to prove by simulating savings on historical BOMs before ever touching a live project.

Since virtually every major ECAD tool exports BOMs as CSV or Excel with a large overlap of common columns (Designator/Reference, Value/Comment, Footprint/Package, Quantity, MPN), the importer is built as one flexible column-mapping engine with ready-made presets for the top 10 tools, rather than ten bespoke parsers — and the optimized BOM is exported back in the same universal format so it can be re-imported into whichever tool the design came from.

title: FileInspector
excerpt: A cross-platform command-line utility (with an optional GUI) that lists files in a directory tree along with their metadata, exporting to JSON, XML, or CSV.
full_description:
FileInspector is a lightweight, cross-platform utility that walks a directory tree and produces a structured inventory of every file it finds — name, path, size, timestamps (created/modified/accessed), and any extended metadata the file format exposes (EXIF for photos, ID3 for audio, page count and author for documents, and so on). Unlike most “list files” utilities, which only export to CSV, FileInspector can output the same scan as JSON, XML, or CSV, so the same tool works equally well feeding a spreadsheet, a script, or a downstream system that expects structured data.

It's loosely inspired by JAM Software's FileList, a long-standing Windows-only command-line tool built for exactly this: generating a directory listing for compliance documentation, inventory audits, and metadata extraction, with filtering by file name, extension, timestamp, directory depth, size, or attributes. FileInspector keeps that same command-line-first design — so it slots into existing scripts, cron jobs, or CI pipelines without any UI — but is written to run identically on macOS, Windows, and Linux, and pairs the CLI with an optional GUI for people who'd rather point-and-click a scan than remember flags.

The GUI isn't a separate product bolted onto the CLI as an afterthought — it's a thin, optional front end that builds the exact same command the CLI accepts, then hands it off, so a scan configured visually can always be reproduced by copying the equivalent CLI invocation into a script later. That single-engine design keeps CLI and GUI results guaranteed identical and avoids maintaining two independent scanning implementations.

Typical use cases: producing an inventory of a shared drive or archive for compliance/audit purposes; documenting exactly what's on a backup before or after it runs, to catch missing or unexpectedly-added files; cataloging a media library (photos/audio/video) by its embedded metadata rather than just filenames; feeding a file inventory into another system (a DAM, an asset-tracking spreadsheet, a data-migration script) via whichever of JSON/XML/CSV that system expects; and forensic/audit trails where a timestamped, exhaustive listing of a directory's exact state needs to be preserved outside the filesystem itself.
features: Cross-platform CLI — identical behavior on macOS, Windows, and Linux
Multi-format output — JSON, XML, and CSV from the same scan
Rich metadata capture — beyond name/size/dates: EXIF (photos), ID3 (audio), document properties (author, page count), and other format-specific fields
Filtering — by file name/extension, timestamp range, directory depth, file size, and file attributes
Optional GUI — builds and runs the same command the CLI accepts, for point-and-click scans
Scriptable — designed to slot into cron jobs, CI pipelines, and existing automation without a UI
Diff/compare mode — compare two scans of the same directory to see what changed
advantages: Cross-platform, where the tool it's loosely based on (FileList) is Windows-only
One tool, three output formats — no separate exporters needed per downstream system
CLI-first design means it automates cleanly; the GUI is additive, not required
Single scanning engine behind both CLI and GUI keeps results identical and halves the maintenance burden
Rich metadata capture turns a plain file listing into a genuinely useful catalog (media libraries, document archives)
Diff/compare mode turns it into a lightweight backup/change-audit tool, not just a one-shot lister
pitfalls: Extracting format-specific metadata (EXIF, ID3, document properties) means bundling or depending on multiple parsing libraries — scope creep risk if every format is chased
Very large directory trees (millions of files) need a streaming/incremental writer, not an in-memory scan, to avoid memory blowup
Cross-platform file-attribute differences (Windows attributes vs POSIX permissions) need a normalized schema so output isn't OS-specific
XML output is rarely anyone's first choice today — worth confirming real demand before investing equal effort in all three formats
GUI must stay strictly a thin wrapper around the CLI, or the two will drift and results will stop matching

title: DealScope
excerpt: A free service: point it at a property listing and say "analyse this deal" — it fetches the property and its comparables, models it as a short-term rental, long-term rental, renovate-and-resell flip or contractual-position assignment, and returns a personalizable PDF report, emailable to whoever needs to see it.
full_description:
DealScope answers a single question that every property buyer asks and almost nobody answers with numbers: given this specific apartment at this specific price, which way of using it actually makes the most money — and how badly does that answer change if the assumptions are wrong? It takes one property, runs it through four different exit strategies side by side, and produces a complete written report on the deal rather than a bare percentage.

The four strategies it models are short-term rental, long-term rental, buy-renovate-resell, and the sale of a contractual position. Short-term rental (Airbnb and equivalents) is driven by nightly rate, seasonal occupancy curves, platform commission, cleaning and linen, utilities, furnishing capex and any licensing the local regime requires. Long-term rental is the quieter model: monthly rent, a vacancy allowance, tenant-default risk, property tax, condo fees, insurance and a maintenance reserve. Buy-renovate-resell is a timeline rather than a yield — purchase, works priced per square metre by scope, a contingency buffer, the holding costs that accrue while the works run long, then selling costs and capital-gains tax. The fourth is the one most tools ignore entirely: buying off-plan and assigning the contractual position before completion, where the return is measured against the deposits actually paid in rather than the full price of the apartment, and where the developer's consent fee, the transfer-tax saving that motivates the incoming buyer, and the completion date are the variables that decide everything.

Underneath the four sits one shared engine, which is what makes the comparison honest. Acquisition costs, transfer tax, stamp duty, notary and registration fees, mortgage terms (LTV, rate, term, and a real amortization schedule rather than a flat interest assumption), the investor's own tax profile and the holding horizon are all entered once and applied identically across every scenario. Each strategy is then reported on the same metrics — net yield, cash-on-cash return, IRR, NPV, payback period, equity multiple, and the break-even point expressed in the terms that matter for that strategy (the occupancy rate, monthly rent, or resale price at which the deal stops making money).

Because no single set of inputs is ever right, every scenario runs as a range instead of a point estimate. Pessimistic, base and optimistic cases run side by side, a tornado chart ranks which assumptions the outcome is genuinely sensitive to, and an optional Monte Carlo pass over the uncertain drivers reports the probability that the deal clears the investor's target return rather than a single confident-looking number. In practice this is the part that changes decisions: it is common for a deal to look best as a short-term rental in the base case and worst in the downside, purely because the model is levered to occupancy.

The intended way to use it is one instruction: point it at a listing and say analyse this deal. From a single URL the tool fetches the property's own details — price, area, typology, location, condition, floor, year of construction, energy rating — and then, without being asked, goes back out and fetches the deal's neighbours: everything currently listed nearby that a buyer would weigh against it. That second fetch is the whole point. A property's numbers mean nothing in isolation; they only become a judgement when set against what else the same money buys on the same streets.

The comparable set is assembled by rule rather than by eye — same locality or a radius around the coordinates, same typology, area within a tolerance band, comparable condition, listed recently enough to still reflect the market — and then reported as a distribution rather than an average: median price per square metre, the spread around it, and the percentile the subject property occupies within its own comp set. Where a snapshot history exists, it adds what a one-off scrape cannot see — which comparables have cut their asking price and by how much, how long the current stock has been sitting, and how quickly listings disappear, which is the closest observable proxy for real absorption in that micro-market.

This is also what turns the financial model from an exercise in guessing into something grounded. Instead of seeded defaults, the comparable set supplies the assumptions directly: achieved rent per square metre from local long-term listings, nightly rates and seasonal occupancy from short-term inventory in the same area, resale values per square metre from the sales comps for the after-repair figure a flip depends on. Every derived assumption stays visible and editable, with the sample it came from attached, so a user who knows the street better than the data can override a number and see the verdict move.

The conclusion the report builds to is therefore a genuine one rather than a yield calculation. It states where the asking price sits against the comp-derived fair band and how much negotiating headroom that implies, ranks the four strategies on returns computed from local evidence, and answers whether the deal is worth doing — with the conditions attached, because the truthful answer is usually conditional: worth it as a long-term rental at the asking price, worth it as a short-term rental only above a given occupancy, not worth it as a flip unless the renovation lands under a stated budget. Where the comparable set is too thin or too scattered to support a conclusion, it says so instead of inventing confidence.

Nothing about that flow is mandatory. Everything can be entered by hand for a property that was never listed publicly, market assumptions come pre-seeded per location as editable defaults when no usable comparables exist, and the listing fetch reuses the extraction schema VC-005 PropInsight is built around — so a first pass takes a price and a postcode, a serious pass takes fifteen minutes of overriding defaults with real quotes, and a scraped dataset can be pushed through the same pipeline in bulk to rank a whole market instead of one apartment.

The output is a proper report, not a dashboard that disappears when the tab closes: a PDF containing the assumption set in full, a strategy comparison table, per-scenario cash-flow waterfalls, a cumulative cash position chart over the holding period, the mortgage amortization table, sensitivity tornadoes and break-even charts, and a plain-language summary of which strategy wins and under what conditions it stops winning. The report downloads directly or is emailed on completion, which matters for the real use case — these get forwarded to a spouse, a business partner, an accountant or a lender, and a document with its assumptions printed on the first page is something another person can actually argue with.

It is meant to be free, and free without an asterisk: no paywalled tier, no report that renders the interesting half blurred, no account required to run an analysis and read the result. A donation button sits on the finished report and nowhere else — visible at the moment the tool has actually been useful to someone, rather than in front of the thing they came for. Donations fund running costs and nothing about them unlocks a feature, because the moment a donation buys something the tool stops being free and starts being a subscription with extra steps. An optional account exists only so that returning users can find their past reports; it is never a condition of using the thing.

Two audiences want this, and they sit on opposite sides of the same table. An estate agent uses it as an advisory tool: running the numbers on a flat before a viewing, then handing the client a report that explains what the property actually yields under each strategy — which is a materially better pitch than forwarding listing photos, and is most of what separates an agent who advises from one who merely lists. A buyer uses it as negotiating armour: a report stating that the asking price sits in the 85th percentile of its own comparable set, that four similar flats nearby have already cut their price, and that the numbers only work below a certain figure, is a far harder thing to wave away across a table than an opinion that the price seems high. The negotiation-headroom figure the verdict already produces is precisely the artifact a buyer puts in front of a broker to justify an offer under asking.

Serving both sides only works if the tool refuses to take one. The report says the same thing about a property regardless of who ran it — there is no agent mode that softens the comparables or a buyer mode that sharpens them — because the instant a report's conclusion depends on who paid for it, it is worth nothing to either side, and the buyer's trust is the asset the agent is borrowing when they attach their logo to it. The practical consequence is that an agent will only forward reports on properties whose numbers genuinely stand up, which is the correct outcome. It also constrains the personalization: a sender can choose which sections to include, but an omitted section is named as omitted, and the shareable link always resolves to the complete analysis, so the format cannot be used to quietly delete the unflattering half.

Reports are personalizable, because most of them are not read by the person who ran them. Someone analysing an apartment is nearly always about to forward the result to a spouse, a business partner, an accountant, a mortgage broker or a client, so the report carries the sender's name and optionally their logo, an editable cover note in their own words, a choice of which sections to include or leave out, and a currency and language setting. The finished thing can be downloaded as a PDF or emailed straight to the recipient with a shareable link to the live version, so an estate agent can send a prospective buyer a genuine numbers-first analysis of the flat they just viewed.

Letting an anonymous visitor send a branded PDF to any address they like is, viewed unkindly, a well-designed spam cannon, so that path needs guarding from the first line of code: the sender's own address is verified before anything can be sent from it, recipients are capped per report and per sender per day, the free-text cover note is length-limited and scanned, every outbound mail carries a clear statement of who triggered it and a one-click way for the recipient to block further mail, and sending runs on its own subdomain with its own reputation so that a burst of abuse cannot take the rest of the service's mail down with it.

Every analysis is stored: the inputs as submitted, the comparable set as it looked at that moment, the derived assumptions, the computed results and the verdict, keyed by a report id. The immediate reason is user-facing — a stored report has a durable link, can be reopened months later, and can be re-run against fresh comparables to show how the same deal has moved. The longer-term reason is that this accumulates into something no individual user could assemble: a record of the deals real people are actually evaluating, which locations and price brackets draw the most attention, and which strategy wins how often under honest local assumptions.

That database needs a way to look at it, so an internal tool ships alongside the service rather than being improvised later against raw SQL: browse and search stored analyses, filter by location, price band, strategy or date, open any individual report exactly as its user saw it, and read the aggregates on top — volume over time, the locations and typologies being analysed most, the distribution of verdicts, donation conversion, and the operational numbers that matter for a free service, namely which site profiles have started failing extraction and what the scraping and email costs are running at. It is also the abuse console: rate-limit violations, suspicious sending patterns and blocked recipients surface here.

Storing all of that carries obligations that are easy to postpone and expensive to retrofit. The records contain personal data — email addresses of senders and recipients, specific property addresses, and what amounts to a stranger's private financial planning — so the service states plainly what it keeps and for how long, applies a retention window rather than hoarding indefinitely, separates the identifying fields from the deal data so the market-level dataset can be analysed and published in aggregate without exposing anyone, and offers deletion on request as a working feature rather than a paragraph in a policy. Free does not mean the user is the product.

Tax and regulatory rules live in per-jurisdiction configuration files rather than being hardcoded, because transfer-tax bands, capital-gains treatment, rental-income taxation and short-term-let licensing differ by country and change with every budget. The tool is explicitly a modelling aid and not financial or tax advice: it shows its work, prints every assumption it used, and is designed so that a professional reviewing the report can see exactly which number to challenge.
